name: Listener crossword No 93: Our Christmas Card

clue.text: 'Here's Christmas — let us … greet him We may as well, for none can cheat him'

definitions.text: 'Here's Christmas — let us … greet him We may as well, for none can cheat him'

blocks.clueFragment: 'Here's Christmas — let us … greet him We may as well, for none can cheat him'
blocks.note: surface reading: a couplet of old Christmas verse with a word missing
setter's reading: the gap wants the adverb saying how we should welcome the season, fearlessly and without holding back

explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation, a common device in early Listener puzzles: the answer is the word the poet wrote where the dots stand.
explanation.definitionFit: The couplet urges meeting Christmas without fear, since nobody can deceive him anyway, so the missing adverb means fearlessly or confidently.

clue.text: The more they are, the merrier they'll be

definitions.text: The more they are, the merrier they'll be

blocks.clueFragment: The more they are, the merrier they'll be
blocks.note: surface reading: the proverb about company, 'the more the merrier'
setter's reading: carol singers going door to door are given drink at each house, so the more of them, the jollier the party

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the more the merrier' is bent to describe Christmas carol singers, who were traditionally plied with drink at every door.
explanation.definitionFit: Waits were bands of street singers and musicians who went round at Christmas performing carols for money and hospitality.

blocks.note: surface reading: a seasonal card or written salutation
setter's reading: a bow or curtsy made as a mark of respect

explanation.walkthrough: On a Christmas card the phrase suggests a written greeting, but the answer is the bodily kind: a bow or bending of the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: A deferential bow or curtsy is a gesture of respect offered when meeting someone of rank.

clue.text: (rev.), 24 Michaelmas is more this than Christmas

definitions.text: Michaelmas is more this than Christmas

indicators.note: the setter's bracketed instruction to write this light backwards, from right to left, in the grid

blocks.clueFragment: Michaelmas is more this than Christmas
blocks.note: the traditional Michaelmas dinner is roast goose, while Christmas has turkey, so the answer is the adjective for goose-like

explanation.surface: A comparison of two English feast days, Michaelmas at the end of September and Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: The word ANSERINE is split across 10 and 24, and only the 10 part is entered backwards. Michaelmas (29 September) is traditionally celebrated in England with roast goose.
explanation.definitionFit: Anserine is the Latin-derived adjective for goose-like, and goose rather than turkey is the bird of the Michaelmas table.

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, used in the phrase 'of yore'

blocks.note: surface reading: nostalgia for a merrier Christmas long past
setter's reading: a single archaic noun for time long gone

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is almost always met in the phrase 'days of yore', meaning long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic noun for time long past, the bygone era people remember fondly.

clue.text: (anag.) 'At Christmas I no more desire a rose Than wish a snow in … new-fangled shows'

definitions.text: 'At Christmas I no more desire a rose Than wish a snow in … new-fangled shows'

blocks.clueFragment: 'At Christmas I no more desire a rose Than wish a snow in … new-fangled shows'
blocks.note: surface reading: a couplet of verse about wanting things out of season, with a word missing
setter's reading: the gap wants the possessive of the late spring month, whose fresh blooms are the new-fangled shows

explanation.walkthrough: The couplet is Berowne's in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost: 'Than wish a snow in May's new-fangled mirth'. The missing word is MAY'S, and the bracketed instruction says to enter it with its letters rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow in late spring would be as unseasonable as a rose in December, so the possessive of that spring month fills the quoted gap.

clue.text: (rev.) It seems the tax may spoil its cheer

definitions.text: It seems the tax may spoil its cheer

blocks.clueFragment: It seems the tax may spoil its cheer
blocks.note: surface reading: a grumble that the government is ruining the festive season
setter's reading: the drink whose cheering effect is threatened by a heavy duty on beer

explanation.walkthrough: Beer duty was raised sharply in Britain in 1931, the year before this puzzle. The answer is entered backwards, as the bracketed instruction says.
explanation.definitionFit: Ale is beer, the traditional Christmas drink of good cheer, and its price was pushed up by the duty levied on it.

clue.text: (rev.) The tinsel on the tree does

definitions.text: The tinsel on the tree does

blocks.clueFragment: The tinsel on the tree does
blocks.note: surface reading: the glittering decoration catching the light
setter's reading: a Scots verb for what tinsel does in a draught, twirling and quivering

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Scots dialect verb, entered backwards as the bracketed instruction says.
explanation.definitionFit: Tirl is Scots for to twirl, spin or vibrate, which is how strands of tinsel move on the branches.

clue.text: Our best wishes that your presents may be

definitions.text: Our best wishes that your presents may be

blocks.clueFragment: Our best wishes that your presents may be
blocks.note: surface reading: the closing line of a Christmas card
setter's reading: an adjective completing the sentence, telling how generous the gifts should be

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a sentence with its last word missing; the answer is the adjective that completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lavish gifts are generous and extravagant, which is what the sender hopes the recipient's presents will be.

blocks.note: surface reading: a feast with something turned on a spit
setter's reading: a young bullock, the beast of the traditional village ox-roast

explanation.walkthrough: An ox-roast, a whole beast turned on a spit, was a traditional English way of feeding a crowd at a fair or celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A stot is a dialect word for a young bullock or steer, an animal that might be spit-roasted whole for a crowd.

clue.text: At this season do it to the kill-joy

blocks.clueFragment: At this season do it to the kill-joy
blocks.note: surface reading: seasonal advice about the guest who spoils the fun
setter's reading: a verb for what should be done with the spoilsport, namely throw him out

explanation.walkthrough: 'It' stands for the answer, a verb: what you should do at Christmas to anyone who spoils the fun.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone is to eject or expel them, the fate wished on a gloomy spoilsport at a party.

clue.text: (rev.), 25 (rev.) Flower not likely to deck our Christmas table

indicators.note: the setter's bracketed instruction that both parts of this light are written backwards in the grid

linkWords: not likely to deck our Christmas table

blocks.note: an old poetic name for the lotus

explanation.surface: A table decorator rejecting a bloom unsuited to a winter feast.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is split between 34 and 25, and each part is entered backwards. The lotus is a summer water flower, not one found in December.
explanation.definitionFit: Lote is an archaic poetic form of lotus, the water lily of Egypt and of the lotus-eaters in Homer.

blocks.note: a short word for long past, close in sense to the answer at 11 across
setter's aside: the entry in the grid is a rearrangement of that word

explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is YORE. The word meaning much the same is AGO, and the grid takes a rearrangement of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ago means in the past, and yore is the time long past, so the two words are near synonyms.

clue.text: This pet would make a lovely present

definitions.text: This pet would make a lovely present

blocks.clueFragment: This pet would make a lovely present
blocks.note: surface reading: a puppy under the tree
setter's reading: a particular lapdog breed of Chinese origin

explanation.walkthrough: The clue simply describes a small dog that might be given as a gift; the answer is the short name for one breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Peke is the short form of Pekingese, a small long-haired toy dog originally bred at the Chinese imperial court.

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; the clue names the kind of Christmas it describes

blocks.note: surface reading: an authentic, old-fashioned festive season
setter's reading: the proper picture-card Christmas is the one with snow on the ground

explanation.walkthrough: A 'real' Christmas in the popular imagination is a white one, so the answer is the adjective for snowy.
explanation.definitionFit: Nival comes from Latin nix, nivis, and describes anything snowy or growing among snow, as a picture-postcard Christmas is.

clue.text: (rev.) Half the rustle of a dress in blind-man's buff

definitions.text: Half the rustle of a dress

blocks.clueFragment: Half the rustle of a dress
blocks.note: the first half of the doubled word for the swish of skirts
setter's aside: playing the party game, the word is turned about, as the blindfolded player is spun round

explanation.surface: A party game in which the blindfolded player follows the sound of a skirt brushing past.
explanation.walkthrough: The rustle is FROU-FROU; half of it is FROU. Blind-man's buff, the game where a blindfolded player is spun round, accounts for its entry backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Frou-frou is the imitative word for the swishing sound of silk skirts, so one half of it is one of the two repeated syllables.

blocks.note: surface reading: the last line of a carol sung at Christmas
setter's reading: Dickens's story of Scrooge, which closes on Tiny Tim's blessing

explanation.walkthrough: The italic title is Dickens's novella, not a carol to sing. Its final words are Tiny Tim's toast, spread across 40, 30 and 33.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens ends his ghost story with the crippled boy Tiny Tim's blessing, the most quoted line in the book.

clue.text: Saturday's postman will help you solve this

definitions.text: Saturday's postman will help you solve this

blocks.clueFragment: Saturday's postman will help you solve this
blocks.note: surface reading: the postman bringing the answers to the puzzle
setter's reading: that Saturday was 26 December, when the postman calls for his seasonal tip

explanation.walkthrough: 26 December 1931 fell on a Saturday. Boxing Day is the British holiday after Christmas, named for the 'Christmas box', a seasonal tip given to tradesmen such as the postman.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christmas box is a gift of money to the postman, collected around the holiday that is named after it.

blocks.note: surface reading: any present given on 1 January
setter's reading: the old word for a present given for luck at the start of a new year

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an old spelling of handsel, entered backwards as the bracketed instruction says. In Scotland the first Monday of the year was Handsel Monday.
explanation.definitionFit: A hansel or handsel is a gift given at the New Year or at a new beginning to bring good luck.

definitions.note: these courses are only the first half of the full meal

blocks.note: surface reading: the opening courses of a Christmas meal
setter's reading: these courses are the first half of the evening meal, so the answer is the first half of that meal's name

explanation.walkthrough: Starters, soup and fish make up the first part of dinner, so the answer is the first part of the word DINNER. It also happens to mean a loud noise, as a crowded table makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The early courses are the front end of the meal, and these letters are the front end of the meal's name.

clue.text: The taste of the cranberry sauce

definitions.text: The taste of the cranberry sauce
definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing that taste

blocks.clueFragment: The taste of the cranberry sauce
blocks.note: surface reading: the flavour of the relish served with turkey
setter's reading: a dialect adjective for a harsh, sharp, sourish flavour

explanation.walkthrough: Cranberries are tart, and the answer is an old dialect adjective for a rough, sharp taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarrish is a dialect word meaning harsh, dry or sour-tasting, which fits a tart berry relish.

clue.text: Old caress, most of it is too shy to

linkWords: most of it is too shy to

blocks.note: an archaic verb, also spelt accoy, meaning to soothe or fondle

blocks.clueFragment: most of it is too shy to
blocks.note: setter's aside: the last three of the four letters form a word for bashful, and a bashful person would not dare

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned endearment that a timid suitor cannot bring himself to give.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic answer is defined plainly; the joke is that three quarters of it spells COY, so most of the word is itself too shy to caress.
explanation.definitionFit: Acoy, or accoy, is a Spenserian verb meaning to calm, soothe or pet someone, which is close to caressing them.

blocks.note: surface reading: an ancient Christmas tradition
setter's reading: the Greek word for law and custom, personified as a goddess

explanation.walkthrough: In a Christmas puzzle this looks like an old festive tradition, but the answer is a Greek word.
explanation.definitionFit: Themis in ancient Greek meant established law or custom, and was personified as the Titan goddess of divine order.

blocks.note: surface reading: skating or skiing as a favourite division of winter athletics
setter's reading: a literal sprig hung up for the seasonal game of kissing beneath it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Branch' suggests a division of a sport, but it is a real sprig, and the 'sport' is kissing under it at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprigs of this parasitic evergreen plant are hung at Christmas, and anyone standing under one may be kissed.

clue.text: Find its thread by reversing it

blocks.clueFragment: Find its thread by reversing it
blocks.note: surface reading: advice to a solver to work a puzzle backwards
setter's reading: the word's old sense of a ball of yarn, the thread that guided Theseus out of the labyrinth

explanation.walkthrough: The answer means both a crossword hint and, in its old sense (also spelt clew), a ball of thread. The clue tells you to enter it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue was originally a ball of thread, and from the thread that led out of the maze came the sense of a guide to a solution.

clue.text: We hope your turkey is not this and the middle of 22

definitions.text: We hope your turkey is not this

blocks.clueFragment: We hope your turkey is not this
blocks.note: surface reading: the cook hopes the bird is not underdone
setter's reading: the centre four letters of 22 across complete a Latin phrase meaning a bird seldom seen

explanation.walkthrough: The middle of LAVISH (22 across) is AVIS; with the answer it makes RARA AVIS, Latin for 'rare bird'. A Christmas turkey should be neither scarce nor undercooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Rara is the Latin feminine for rare, and joined to avis it makes the proverbial rare bird, punning on a rare turkey.

blocks.note: surface reading: any bloom used to decorate at the season
setter's reading: the plant popularly called the Christmas rose, which flowers in midwinter

explanation.walkthrough: The Christmas rose is not a rose at all but a white-flowered plant that blooms in December.
explanation.definitionFit: Helleborus niger, the black hellebore, is commonly known as the Christmas rose because it blooms in midwinter.

clue.text: Its anagram often comes out of a Christmas cracker

definitions.text: often comes out of a Christmas cracker

blocks.clueFragment: often comes out of a Christmas cracker
blocks.note: surface reading: the motto, toy or joke inside a pulled cracker
setter's aside: the grid takes a rearrangement of the word for the paper headgear, a bishop's tall pointed hat

explanation.walkthrough: A Christmas cracker is a paper tube pulled apart at the British dinner table; it holds a paper hat, often shaped like a bishop's. The grid takes an anagram of that hat's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Paper hats in crackers were often made in the shape of a bishop's tall pointed headdress.

blocks.note: surface reading: a disorderly Christmas party
setter's reading: wild merrymaking, the word then muddled in the grid

explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' does double duty: it describes the merrymaking and tells you the entry is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Riot in its old sense means loose, noisy festivity and wild merrymaking, as in 'running riot'.

blocks.note: surface reading: the other half of the dress's swish from 39 across
setter's reading: a different, Scots, word for a rustle, cut in half

explanation.walkthrough: After 39 across took half of one rustling word, this takes the first half of another: fissle, a Scots word meaning to rustle.
explanation.definitionFit: Fissle is a Scots verb meaning to rustle or make a faint stirring sound, and these letters are its front half.

definitions.note: the answer names the kind of island it is

blocks.note: surface reading: the Pacific island named for the day it was found
setter's reading: the type of island, a coral ring around a lagoon

explanation.walkthrough: Christmas Island in the Pacific, sighted by Captain Cook on Christmas Eve 1777, is a coral reef ring around a lagoon.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral island enclosing a lagoon, and Kiritimati, the Pacific Christmas Island, is the largest one.

blocks.note: surface reading: the chorus of a carol coming round again
setter's reading: a printed musical sign in the score that shows where a repeat begins or ends

explanation.walkthrough: In sheet music, a repeat is often marked with a sign, and the answer is that sign's Italian name.
explanation.definitionFit: The segno, Italian for sign, is the notation symbol showing the point from which a passage is to be repeated.

blocks.note: surface reading: a cross-reference sending you to an earlier clue
setter's reading: the clue's own last word is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing above to see: the answer is simply the last word of the clue, entered jumbled as the bracketed note says.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue names its own answer, so the word sits literally in the cross-reference phrase meaning higher on the page.

clue.text: Listener finds 5 this when more becomes less

definitions.text: Listener finds 5 this when more becomes less

blocks.clueFragment: Listener finds 5 this when more becomes less
blocks.note: surface reading: a radio listener judging the carol singers
setter's reading: rewrite the clue at 5 with 'less' for 'more', and the fewer singers the better

explanation.walkthrough: The Listener was the BBC's weekly magazine; this one is a person listening. Change 5's clue to 'The less they are, the merrier' and it gives the listener's view of the singers.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial is a nuisance or annoyance to be put up with, which is how out-of-tune singers at the door strike a listener.

blocks.note: surface reading: a child's Christmas morning disappointment
setter's reading: the adjective describing a stocking with nothing in it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Such' stands for the answer, an adjective: a stocking with nothing in it on Christmas morning would be a tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Void means empty or containing nothing, the state of a stocking that Father Christmas has missed.

blocks.note: surface reading: any time of year
setter's reading: in a Christmas puzzle, the old name for the festive period itself

explanation.walkthrough: In a Christmas puzzle 'the season' can only mean one thing; the answer is its old Germanic name.
explanation.definitionFit: Yule is the old word for the midwinter Christmas festival, as in yule log and yuletide.

clue.text: (anag.) When you're in this your goose is cooked

definitions.text: When you're in this your goose is cooked

blocks.clueFragment: When you're in this your goose is cooked
blocks.note: surface reading: the Christmas goose on the stove
setter's reading: the idiom for being in trouble, which is also something a bird can be cooked in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Your goose is cooked' means you are done for, and so does being 'in the soup'. The word is entered jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the soup is an idiom for being in serious trouble, the same plight as having one's goose cooked.

blocks.note: surface reading: the cavity of the roast bird
setter's reading: the middle of the name of the Christmas bird, where stuffing goes

explanation.walkthrough: Stuffing goes inside the turkey, and the inside of TURKEY is URK. It is entered backwards as the bracketed note says.
explanation.definitionFit: The stuffing is packed into the bird's centre, and these three letters are the centre of the bird's name.
